Question of the Day #204: Where on the Sliding Scale of Idealism vs. Cynicism do you like stories?

link_counts.title: Sliding Scale of Idealism vs. Cynicism - TV Tropes

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
Definitely leaning further towards the Idealism end of the scale, for me. I greatly prefer positive messages and people.

Mostly to make up for my own internal tendency towards cynicism, as I don’t want to deal with the consequences of wallowing in that negativity… again.

About 70% cynic is probably my average. I don’t want to go full bleak nihilist, but I have a low tolerance for willful ignorance, pollyanna cheerfulness, and apologism for the necessity of evil in the world as being part of some sort of divine plan or cosmic order. I think we live in a crapsack world because people choose to keep making it that way (admittedly some of our problems come from nature, but I think if we made all people stop acting like idiots, we’d have the power necessary to scientifically fix all those natural issues). So I like stories that acknowledge the unarguable fact that life kinda sucks most all of the time, but leaves the door open a couple inches for the possibility that things could become better someday. The writer Kurt Vonnegut is a pretty good scale by which to calibrate my preferences, although he’s a bit more liberal than I would prefer, and I don’t agree with all of his solutions. But his ability to analyze the problems, and the general tone of sardonic humor he sets, put him pretty solidly in my top 5 writers of all time.

The_Justifier:

I have a low tolerance for willful ignorance, pollyanna cheerfulness, and apologism for the necessity of evil in the world as being part of some sort of divine plan or cosmic order.

Well, to me at least, none of those things are Idealism. It’s not willful ignorance, but rather acknowledging bad stuff, but striving for better things nonetheless. And there could certainly be a no-nonsense, serious idealist, in my opinion. Nor do I think Idealism necessitates believing in the “necessity of evil.”

QotD #204 Reply: Definitely on the idealistic side. A good dose or two of Cynicism every now and again helps to keep stories interesting, but I still prefer hopeful Idealism to gloomy Cynicism. In short, Silly Rabbit, Cynicism Is for Losers!, no offense intended.

Cynicism doesn’t equal Realism, and Idealism doesn’t equal Optimism.

The_Justifier:

The list of Principles doesn’t tell me what a Principle actually is; the term suggests an ideology or moral framework, but the list items make it seem more like a powerset.

Yeah, it’s kinda both. Principles are, basically, the two most important aspects of a given Hero (conceptually, not mechanically). Sometimes one of those aspects is an ideology, sometimes it’s a power. For instance, Legacy has the Principles of the Hero and Justice, because being heroic and dishing out Justice are what define her. Sure, she could have the Principles of Strength and the Indestructible instead, but those powers are far less important to Legacy as a character. On the other hand, the Wraith has the Principle of Stealth, because that capability is a major aspect of her character.

The_Justifier:

if it’s about gaining some ability to actually do things

It’s not, really. It’s more about getting better at things you can already do. Principle of the Time Traveler, e.g., wouldn’t let you travel in time by itself, but it would make you better at Time-related tasks (think Timeslinger). If you had the Time Travel Power, though, the Principle would make you better at using that Power. (Although no Time Travel Power actually exists in the game, for semi-obvious fiction and game-balance reasons. One could easily add such a Power, though . . . )

fjur:

Yeah, I agree that, mechanically, the Shackles are quite potent and useful, but narratively they don’t seem to make a whole lotta sense to me. Why is Tempest carrying them around all the time?

Contrary to Rabit, I don’t think it’s wrong to say that a person who was transformed by a trial that they went through would not want to carry a memento of that experience. Characterizing it as “trauma” is a viewpoint common to the modern social paradigm, but many past generations thought more about a crucible, which burned away their weakness and left only the pure core of who they were. A common trope example is that of a gangster who survived being shot because a whiskey flask in his pocket caught the bullet that would otherwise have gone in his heart, and he keeps the flask with the bullet in it thereafter to remind himself of that brush with death. Nearly dying could be an experience that someone is traumatized by, but it doesn’t have to be; some people would draw strength from the knowledge that they survived, rather than collapsing in a panic because they almost didn’t.

And how does whipping them out and reflecting on his hatred of GW Voss make him better at zapping, e.g., Omnitron?

It represents the fact that he’ll do anything necessary to oppose a tyrant, someone who succeeds through pure strength and oppresses those weaker than themself. Highest HP is the best proxy for “strongest” in this game system. The best question about the shackles is why he needs to physically have them, rather than simply remembering the incident, but this can easily be answered; maybe he feels a physical pain from having the shackles on, and that pain focuses his mind and gives him a little bit of a berserker rage to tap into. We also don’t know a lot of the details about how the gene-binding process works, so there may well be aspects of physical transformation inherent in that.

Hargomme was a character in an Amber campaign that used a variation on Everway (a diceless game system). Likely a child of Eric (for those who know Amber lore), he grew up ignorant of his origins as a servant in a royal household and a soldier, but eventually earned positions as general in the royal mounted forces and and royal spy master before encountering Amberites and being taken away from his home to roam shadow with some others like himself, where they had many adventures and discoveries about both reality and themselves.

My favorite RPG character is myself… give me a long moment, and I shall explain.

When I was about 15 I discovered a game called Mage the Ascension, where you play modern day wizards in a noirish urban fantasy version of Earth, and one of the earliest practice character creation exercises I did was to imagine how my actual life history could have prompted me to join one of the nine factions of wizards in the game (eg if I’d stayed with my intellectual wannabe-science teacher of a father, I’d have wound up as one of the mad scientists who use magic to enforce obsolete pseudoscience theories, while moving in with my neopagan mother instead steered me more toward being one of the sinister super-witches whose power comes from blood rituals and twisted trees). Later in life, as my childish idealism gave way to a more Nietzschean worldview, I also did versions of myself for the game’s “bad guy” factions.

And eventually I decided that all these splinter versions of the same basic personality, who developed different magical practices and powers because of differing life experiences, were all the result of one original wizard, whose life was the same as mine, but who eventually completed the RPG’s “ascend to near-godhood” option. And his version of becoming nigh-omnipotent was to go back through his (my) personal history, figure out every other possible path his life could have taken, and take all of them.

(This rather parallels the way I play SOTM; I’ve always thought that what makes that “Multiverse” in the name is so perfect, is that when you backtrack through a SOTM game that you’ve played, something I used to do a lot when trying to fix errors, even the smallest changes quickly compound on one another, producing a radically different result. You’re told to pick between two heroes that are tied for highest HP to take a bunch of damage, you decide somewhat arbitrarily which one tanks that hit, then a single card play pops out a bunch of minions that all attack the lowest HP, and the one who was tied for highest a minute ago is suddenly KOed. Rewinding and letting the other hero be the one to go down instead can really heavily influence whether the survivor has any hope of pulling off the win.)

Question of the Day #228: Would you want to be cursed with permanent, un-switchable invisibility?

I fully expect that this (along with intangibility) is a likely outcome of IRL death - the classic “ghost” scenario - so I have no particular fear of it, and can very definitely see advantages that I would enjoy exploiting. I think it would be no worse than the condition we’re currently living in, and it might be better, depending on the exact details of how it works (eg probably no hunger, that’s a definite plus, and possibly no fatigue, which would be a minus if it still applied, etc. etc.).

If it’s just invisibility, as with the movie “Hollow Man”, my behavior would probably be similar to that character, albeit a little less openly psychotic (but still fairly predatory, largely out of necessity, since I would no longer have access to the societal mechanisms that enable one to support oneself in a prosocial fashion). I wouldn’t be compelled to act like a Hollywood bad guy, but I would go a little power-mad, partly because I already am mad from lack of power, and partially because of the limited truth behind the extremely overused canard “power corrupts”. It’s not really the power itself which causes the corruption directly; rather, a powerful person tends to become socially isolated, and because we are a species that depends on social bonds to form our sanity, anything which severs us from socialization also erodes our personal foundations.

PS: Ultimately what makes the Hollow Man concept function as a literary trope is the fact that whoever has created the invisibility technology picks some sort of criminal to test it on, because they’re unwilling to kill some loyal soldier by using him as a guinea pig. But by using someone equivalent to what the SCP Foundation calls a “D-class”, you always run the risk that the disposable person you’ve disposed of will not actually go away, and will in fact end up becoming a lot more dangerous to you because of this mistreatment. (The Apotheosis canon segment of the SCP wiki explores this concept in great detail.) The title character in Hollow Man was already a monster even before he gained monstrous power, because of the way that he was rejected by the world around them. Granted, invisibility is a “total villain power” by nature, as Freddy Freeman pointed out, but mind control is often thought of as similarly sinister, and Professor X proves that it doesn’t always have to be. Thusly, if someone along the lines of Captain America had been permanently stuck as the Invisible Thing instead of Sue and Ben, it’s unlikely that Invisi-Steve would go sneaking into women’s bedrooms and having his way with them, as we see HM doing.

(PPS: I honestly thought that the original Invisible Man from the H.G. Wells story was also a criminal like HM, but apparently this confusion comes from either the book or the movie of “League of Extraordinary Gentlemen”, which seemingly pretty much uses HM in place of Wells’s vision of the character. I wish I could track down exactly when I first got these two wildly different stories so thoroughly entangled in my mind, to the point that it’s now nearly impossible for me to separate them.)

Question of the Day #236: You can only have the SotM Core Set and one expansion. Which one do you choose? We’re assuming EE, for obvious reasons. Rook City, Infernal Relics, Shattered Timelines, and Wrath of the Cosmos sold separately. The Mini-expansions and variants are included in the set they were originally released with.

Infernal Relics. Nightmist is one of my three favorite heroes, Argent is also fun, and three of the four villains are in my top ten. The environments kinda suck, but you can’t have everything. Vengeance and OblivAeon give you more heroes to choose from, and the latter is really tempting because it also contains five environments, but if you only have the core set plus OblivAeon, you’re going to get really tired of fighting the same four villains over and over (I should know, I did exactly this after purchasing the app last year). The Big O doesn’t actually hit the table often enough to be a good investment, and the same is true to a lesser extent with the V5 (plus only two Environments…if it had three more then we’d be at an even 30, and then I might consider it in order to get Natch and the Sentinels). Wrath of the Cosmos is the only other one that’s even tempting; RC is just kind of awful as a set, with only three really good decks in it, and Shattered Timelines has two excellent heroes but only two villains that aren’t hair-tearing-out levels of unpleasant to go up against. (And VOTM has no heroes at all, so even though it gives you lots of variety in opponents, I can’t even consider it.)

Villains of the Multiverse has no Heroes, so no. And Vengeance has no single-Deck Villains, so also no. The Organisation, The Matriarch, and Rook City are all pretty tough, and Mister Fixer, Expatriette, and Spite aren’t the most balanced/fun decks, so let’s say no to Rook City. I like NightMist and AA, but they are very complex, and Apostate is kinda a drag, so I’ll cross off Infernal Relics. OblivAeon is very tempting, with five Heroes and Environments each . . . but the Villain itself doesn’t have much mileage. Let’s see, of the remaining two sets (WotC & ST), I think I can’t find any preferences regarding any of the Heroes or Environments. Regarding Villains, each set has one very tough opponent (Progeny and IL) . . . erm, I guess I’ll go with Shattered Timelines, as (for me, at least) the Villains in Wrath of the Cosmos are, on average, more difficult. Mind you, this isn’t me say that Shattered Timelines is “the best set,” or any such thing. I don’t really think that there’s one set that’s completely better than all the others.

There are several more obscure races that premiered after D&D was bought by Wizards of the Coast, which I find far more interesting than the standard Tolkien knock-offs of original D&D, or even the handful of 2E creations such as tieflings or Thri-Kreen, all of which are describable in a sentence or two. I’m going to give three possible choices, depending on just how indulgent the “Dungeon Master” is when transforming me into one of them (a la the D&D cartoon).

#3 - Shardmind. I don’t actually know the details of this species, as they came from the 4th Edition, which I never played. But they’re some sort of inorganic living crystal creature with natural psionic abilities, so I’m automatically interested. Even if their innate abilities are useless, just not having to eat or perhaps even breathe would be reason enough for me to enjoy being one of them.

#2 - Spellscale. From Races of the Dragon, this species of natural sorcerers have thin dragon-like scales but are still pretty human-looking, which is “best of both worlds” stuff from my perspective. However, one of their main racial abilities is that they can pray to a different one of the dragon deities every day, gaining special powers particular to that god’s particular portfolio. I wouldn’t want to be a spellscale if these deities didn’t actually exist, at least enough that meditating on their concept wouldn’t grant the powers involved. And given that I myself have always ruled that dragons shouldn’t HAVE gods, whenever I’m the DM, it would be highly surprising if I found myself able to draw power from such entities.

#1 - Changeling. From the Eberron campaign setting. No powerset is of greater interest to me than shape-shifting, and these half-doppelgangers can automatically change their appearance completely, with all the indications being that it’s not a merely skin-deep pretense, but a complete bodily transformation that will fool even the closest inspection. The ability to reinvent my identity on the fly would be astonishingly useful, particularly given my lack of social graces; every time some disastrous faux pas destroys all my existing friendships, I can take on a new persona and either win back those allies or find new ones. Literally no single superpower would be as useful to me as this (unless “omnipotence” is an option).

Question of the Day #251: Do you care about seeing/hearing spoilers before watching/reading/playing something?

It’s hard to generalize about spoilers. I almost never go see new movies live in the theater (the last time I remember thinking about doing so was in 2019, but I’m unsure whether I actually did it). It’s rare for me to see a film without knowing something about it, so a lot of minor surprises have been spoiled without my caring. For a semi-recent example that’s still old enough that most people probably don’t care, when the trailers for “Spider-Man: Far from Home” came out and revealed a seeming superhero named Mysterio, anyone who knew the comics was going to have a suspicion that this character was probably not what he claimed to be. Knowing this when I finally saw the film earlier this year, I was still able to be blown away by the twist when it actually came, simply because of how good the presentation was; I knew there was a surprise, but what the surprise was exactly was still exciting to discover. But conversely, the well-known movie “The Sixth Sense” is famous for having had a once-mind-blowing twist ending, and now that pretty much everyone knows about that, I’ve never had any strong impulse to go watch it, since the twist was pretty much the whole point of that film. So really, it depends on the exact work, the narrative purpose of the twist, and the expectations surrounding it at the time.

Question of the Day #252: What is the optimal number of players to have in an RPG party?

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
Personally, I find it is somewhere between 1 and 5.

Seriously, not trying to be flippant! There are different benefits to different numbers, in my experience. The focused experience of smaller groups (1-3) is wonderful, while the ability to play off of others in medium-sized groups (3-5) is also great, just in a different way!

I won’t play with more than 5 if I can avoid it, though. Just too many people for me to manage and facilitate as a GM, myself.

In my experience, people drop out all the time, so it’s better to have a large number so that you can deal with no-shows. 5 or 6 is probably good; 6 means harder XP math, if you’re doing that, but otherwise it’s better to have the extra person. If your game only ever has 3 players and 2 of them don’t show up one day, you basically have no game, or a very threadbare one.

My Reply to QotD #252: I agree with @Rabit. If there are few players, then the adventure can generally be more personalized to them. But, like @The_Justifier said, it’s always good to have a buffer if there are no-shows.

Question of the Day #256: Do you read the newspaper?

Relatedly, do you think print is dead?

One day, our rich Western society will no longer be able to sustain its constant growth, and will begin to collapse. Electricity will no longer be cheap and plentiful, and access to the Internet will be a rarity at best. At that time, books will become valuable again.

So my answer to the question of “is print dead” is “that is not dead which can eternal lie*, and with strange aeons, even death may die.”

Newspapers were however always a step or three below books in terms of utility; they’re designed for cheap mass production, not permanence, and so largely replacing them with internet articles makes a bit more sense. We should probably do like a monthly or even weekly publication of information from NetNews articles in book form, for the sake of the historical record, but multiple daily papers all competing for the eyeballs of the public was never an idea that made all that much sense. Until and unless the technological collapse happens, newspapers are not particularly needed.

I read the funny pages about once a week, and an occasional variety article, but in terms of actual happenings, I wouldn’t trust the media to tell me that water is wet, so I don’t have much interest even apart from all my philosophies above.

Footnote - (brary)

Yeah, it seems kinda dumb to store so much vital information on digital systems that could easily become inaccessible.

My Reply to QotD #256: No.

Question of the Day #257: What was the best/worst prank you’ve been victim to or played on someone else?

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
One of the players in a college D&D campaign pulled an April Fool’s joke on the gaming group (which isn’t actually pertinent to this story ), so the rest of the players and I got together and started working on the next year’s event to pull on him. The player’s character was a dwarven warrior named Hendel Rockbiter who wore plate, weilded a magical hammer in one hand and a magical sword in the other, and like to open combat with “Choose your destroyer” while indicating his weapons as the choices.

I maintained notes on all the creatures and NPCs the group had previously dealt with and dealt with over the next year of play, and came up with a weird situation in which this local leader who had screwed over the PCs on their very first adventure (but promptly disappeared never to be seen again) had stolen something from Hendel and was fleeing from the PCs. Hendel had made it a practice of looking for this person everywhere they went, leaving (very bad) drawings of him on home-made “wanted” posters, so I knew it would be a good motivator.

There were three stages to the pursuit, where they would be fighting their entire way through these situations, chasing the thief the entire way:

  1. All the adversaries (except the thief) were generic, like “orcs” or “necromancers”
  2. The adversaries included minor NPCs they had encountered and defeated – but not killed – over the campaign
  3. The adversaries were the powerful villains and other NPCs they had fought and beat – in some cases, killed! – and everyone was trying to destroy the world.

For the day of the game, I made sure the other players knew what we were doing, that this was a “special” game. They played their characters in exaggerated ways, in the ways that Hendel would expect, but dialed up to 11. For example, since Hendel thought the human ranger was clumsy and kinda ridiculous, the player actually played him even more so, lying about rolls so he always failed spectacularly and making spectacularly bad decisions.

I ran the game focusing primarily on Hendel’s player, keeping him focused and attentive on the pursuit of the thief. He was building this theory that the thief had allied with their enemies to take them all down. Over the course of the pursuit, the other PCs were taken out slowly, one-by-one, but Hendel was completely driven to catch the thief, leading him into a massive combat against powerful forces of the gods all bent on global destruction, including his own god, Moradin. He defeated opponent after opponent as the world literally fell apart around him, leaving bodies and debris floating in the vast nothingness of reality.

Finally, I told him after he struck down a powerful foe (I think it was an avatar of Lolth?), that, as he looked around the remains of the battlefield, he realized there were only two entities left alive in the nothingness: Hendel and Moradin. Hendel cheered and made some comments to Moradin about how awesome he was and that they could reforge the world as it should be…

But Moradin turned towards him, a massive hammer in one hand and a powerful, glowing sword in the other, gestured with the weapons, and said “Choose your destroyer.”

Hendel’s move.

The player stared at me in complete awe, still unaware of what was going on and completely in the moment, and the combat started. For a warrior who worships combat, after all, what could be better than fighting your own god?

After a few minutes of this combat (because I realized it was almost midnight!!!), I told him he took a hit of the hammer to his head and, as everything went black, heard…

All of us yelling “April Fool’s Day!!!”

He was completely speechless. Truly.

Once he recovered (and we all stopped laughing over the ridiculousness of everything that had happened and recounting all the fun), I described how Hendel woke up with a horrible headache after a long night of eating, drinking, and brawling that had apparently caused the dream…

Or did it? There was a woman walking away, mumbling in frustration… Before vanishing as though she had never been there. (And yes, I did end up using this as part of a campaign arc. )

That was more than 30 years ago. Hendel’s player still loves talking about that session, describing it as the best TTRPG experience he’s ever had. It even came up a few weeks ago, the last time I talked to him.

That is streets ahead, @Rabit.

Question of the Day #265: What real-world IP would you want creative control over?

Magic the Gathering, absolutely no question. I could make a few improvements to D&D, but with a couple of exceptions like the recent orc debacle, the 5E team has been doing pretty good work; even the two comic universes probably don’t require my help. But the makers of MTG have dropped more balls than the entire history of the NBA, constantly making short-sighted corporate decisions to push profitability, at the cost of damaging the future of the brand.

I have actually worked for the creative team in a small capacity one time, and I flatter myself that them ceasing to return my calls was a small injustice of this sort. But by far the biggest such fumble, which I would immediately work to correct if I wound up owning the company, involves an individual whom I know only as Mercer, the handle he went by on the MTG Salvation forums a little over a decade ago.

Mercer is a fairly talented artist, probably still working in this capacity, and one of his earliest publicized projects was a webcomic called Nascent. This tells the story of Earth becoming a part of the MTG universe, with people in various IRL countries becoming able to intuitively use color magic in a superpower-esque fashion, and following the first such person to become a Planeswalker, traveling to the other worlds that Magic has published. Not only did Mercer have a very innovative imagination, creating such concepts as a humanoid made out of lightning, a race of intelligent beetles, or a swamp with a dark sky that’s lit from below… but more importantly, he showed a very well layered understanding of how the philosophies associated with the five magic colors actually intersect with realistic human psychology. The planeswalker protagonist has a friend whose White-magic inclinations drive her to beat up some schoolyard bullies and get punished, while another of his friends is a goth who carries a switchblade and threatens to murder people who cause trouble for those who “belong” to him, a scary-acting but ultimately benevolent person who was probably being set up as a tragic villain for his former loved ones.

When Magic put out the first bits of information about what would become the New Phyrexia expansion (which, by interesting coincidence, is also the one I worked on, as well as the yearly core set right after it), he was apparently very annoyed by the revisionist history that was applied to the previous Mirrodin setting in order to set up its transformation into NP. The corporate brand team currently in charge of Magic had already had a well established pattern of disregarding previously established lore in favor of their current “unified vision” of the IP franchise, and this was apparently the final straw for Mercer. Not only did he stop playing Magic, but he also stopped making the Nascent webcomic after about 100 pages, and stopped paying for a website to host it on. Thank all that’s holy, I had saved all but maybe two of these pages on my computer, enabling me to binge-read them all once every couple of years; otherwise they would be lost to me forever, and I would be poorer for the lack of this incomplete but brilliant little story.

So if I wound up controlling Magic’s publisher Wizards of the Coast, or preferably its owner the Hasbro corporation, or at bare minimum the MTG department within WotCo, I would do one thing basically first. I would hire Internet-savvy private investigators to track down the actual identity of Mercer (assuming he didn’t just have a Contact Me on his current website), and then show up in a limo and ask for an hour of his time to talk about an old project of his. After providing a groveling apology on behalf of the short-sighted morons who had previously held the authority now possessed by myself, I would then offer to do whichever of two things he would prefer, at any cost I could pay without immediately being fired by the company for bankrupting my whole department overnight. If he had the time or inclinations to raise his own baby, I’d offer to immediately hire him in a role junior only to mine, with respect to the creative department; I might not agree with all of his ideas, but a level of genius such as he displayed deserved to be supported. Alternatively, if he had forgotten MTG completely and didn’t want to relearn it, I would simply offer to purchase the legal rights to Nascent, ask him to summarize any of his ideas he could remember that didn’t make it into the comic during its lifespan (eg confirming or correcting my suspicion that the Goth teenager would end up becoming a nemesis to the planeswalker hero), and leave him with a good sized pile of money and my assurances that I wouldn’t do the creative equivalent of turning his daughter into a prostitute. I would then republish Nascent immediately as one of Magic’s official tie-in comics, create a tie-in set to represent the “Earth with color magic” setting, and begin recruiting the most talented co-writers and artists I could find, in order to continue the Nascent story after this decade-long interruption. (Hey, Doctor Who and Star Trek both had much longer delays before resuming.)

I would fix and alter and otherwise mess with a bunch of other things as well if I owned MTG, but that’s the big one.

Question of the Day #273: Chaos or Order?

All the more reason for me to prefer dogs, filthy and ungentle peasant that I am.

Order can naturally emerge from within Chaos, whereupon it will either crystallize further or be subsumed again. But Order cannot tolerate the existence of Chaos within itself, and will always work to stamp out every last trace of it. For this reason, I am on Team Chaos 100%. Everyone should have the freedom to say (or, in an ideal world, do) literally anything they please… and then, anyone who doesn’t want to hear it has the freedom to stop up their own ears and avoid listening. That’s the kind of fair and reasonable solution that is permitted to exist within a Chaotic system, whereas Order will always work to try and make everything perfectly harmonious and efficient, ruthlessly exterminating any deviation or disruption to their absolutist ideal. By way of analogy, I would rather have hundreds of terrorists bombing random locations all over the world for no reason whatsoever, instead of just a single fanatical organization which has a deliberate plan to completely wipe out my particular kind of creature. The former might have the higher body count, but imo it is far and away the lesser evil.

Over the years, I’ve used all kinds of aids/accessories for various games I’ve run:

  • Minis, including some from Hero Forge (because they are awesome!!! ) and Litko stands to use images of whatever I need instead of spending money / using space on the “real thing”
  • Chessex MEGAMAT (wet and dry erase) that I draw the map on, published/laminated maps (from all kinds of sources), printed-at-home maps (that I cut up and tape back together so they only see what they actually know about - many of my own creation), maps drawn on white boards, digital maps revealed on a TV via computer, digital maps revealed via Fog of World (in Realm Works - although note that they are no longer going to be doing development on RW ), and 3-D constructed maps (to either really sell a major moment or provide better visualization of a non-traditional environment), such as these:

IMG_23201920×2560 330 KB

61920×1440 155 KB

  • Alea Tools for all kinds of uses, but mostly to indicate effects on minis and in combination with the initiative board, below
  • A large, home-made initiative board:
    Initiative_board1920×2560 318 KB
  • A variety of tools for mood music / sound effects, although lately I’ve been exclusively using Syrinscape for that
  • A random NPC generator (originally in Excel but now in Google Sheets) that I created to avoid my own biases around NPC details (e.g., gender, race, names) - The link is a copy that folks can mess with all they like, but it’s always a work-in-progress and since it’s always been just for my use I’ve never cleaned it up or included instructions
  • A workbook we use in our campaign session 0 to ensure everyone is on the same page as to expectations for the game - it’s overkill for most folks, but it’s all things we’ve learned over the years that we have had issues with folks not understanding that ended up impacting our games in a negative way
  • And for atmosphere / effect: Flash paper and flash cotton (to create the effect of something blowing up while RPing as an NPC), candles, red light bulbs (especially for horror-themed games, LED bulbs that can change lights via an app (to really alter a mood at a moment’s notice), and all kinds of physical props and puzzles to challenge and entertain the players:

posts.cooked: Okay, well, as long as Rabit is going to make us all look like a bunch of amateurs, JAQ #2: what is the most ambitious RPG session you’ve ever run?

In running the SC-RPG, yes, I do use cards, but I bought dry-erase cards so they can be reused. (I also got the GM kit, which includes a bunch of pre-printed cards. They are awesome!!! )

I, too, use index cards to run the game. And I’d like to pick up the GM Kit sometime soon, as well.

Wow. I am absolutely awestruck by your dedication to the craft, @Rabit. You are truly among the best of us.

And to answer my own final question(s), I do use a GM Screen, although it’s almost certainly unnecessary, as my notes are just on a laptop.

I do not use any maps or minis; we, instead, simply use the so-called “Theater of the Mind.” I’ve found that it works decently well. But who knows, maybe this will change in the future.

I have not yet used any sound effects, although I was mighty close to playing an ominous thundercrack whenever the name of the local Vampire Lord was spoken, but I couldn’t get it figured out in time. (Although the players have provided, e.g., the sound of hoofbeats by pounding their knuckles against the table.)

The_Justifier:

JAQ #2: what is the most ambitious RPG session you’ve ever run?

Hmm . . . Nothing that I’ve done stands out as particularly ambitious to me (especially when compared to Rabit’s masterful work). I guess I’ll go with the time when I had only ≈40 minutes to run an introductory one-shot for some folks.

Never answered my own first question. The interaction between Supes and Cap was masterfully done in my single favorite mainstream comic of all time, Kurt Busiek’s “JLA vs Avengers”, in which the two immediately see in each other all that is worst about that universe compared to their own (Cap accuses the more powerful and interventionist JLA of stifling humanity’s growth, while Supes is offended that the more street level Marvel heroes get embroiled in politics rather than having a sense of pure moral certainty). Thusly, if both were simultaneously pulled into the SCU, I would have them no longer having that “universal exemplar” status generating friction in them, and they’d immediately get along. They probably wouldn’t quite like Paul the 8th, but they would be more than cooperative in working with him to sort out whatever cosmic wedgie was responsible for their presence in his world.

The_Justifier:
fjur:

although I was mighty close to playing an ominous thundercrack whenever the name of the local Vampire Lord was spoken

So is this Count Strahd, a transparent expy of him (and exactly how transparent), or someone original?

It wasn’t Strahd. I suppose, depending on one’s opinion, he could be considered either (or both) of the latter two. His name was “Lord von Dartus”, which is one letter away from being an anagram of “Strahd.” I’d say that he’s as much an expy of Strahd as he is one of Dracula. He was a pretty stereotypical Vampire. Except he had a twist backstory, in which he was once a legendary heroic Paladin, but than cowardly ran from a battle, so he turned into an Anti-Paladin. So, being ashamed of himself, he hid away in a stereotypical Vampire castle. Oh, and he was never actually a Vampire, he just fabricated that lie so no one would disturb his penance, and to explain his immortality. (He was really immortal because of a blessing he received during his adventuring career.) Also the place in which he lived is called “The Valley of Varobia,” an anagram of Barovia.

That is quite a lot of detail, but you asked for it.

I may, from time to time, post a question in this thread if I have one and lack anywhere else to ask it.

What is your favourite tabletop roleplaying game campaign setting (aside from the Sentinel Comics RPG, of course) for story and lore reasons, not rules and mechanics reasons?

(Also, remember that game ≠ setting. A single RPG can offer multiple different settings.)

Man I completely forgot I was doing Just A Question. Five questions in five days, and then five weeks without. I wonder if it’s worth bothering to resume after a flop like that.

Anyway, my answer would likely be Glorantha if I had ever read it, just based on how beautiful the book is. But since that’s not on my list so far, I have to pick a different answer. Likely candidates are mostly ruled out by being individual sections of a larger interconnected world, where I love the whole but can’t really isolate how much I like the parts (the obvious example being World of Darkness, which isn’t a setting, it’s fifteen settings that are all semi compatible). And of course I rule out any system which is completely generic and has no setting by default, like Big Eyes Small Mouth, probably the prettiest rpg book I own. So I guess I have to go with the coolest thing that’s left. That would probably be…

Well, while the Justifier is busy being eaten by xxt’Hulish, I’ll answer.

It might be Dungeons & Dragons’ Spelljammer, which is just D&D in SPAAAAACE! It’s just so much nonsense. Suffice it to say that I am very excited for its upcoming book.

Other D&D settings that I particularly like are Dark Sun (post-apocalyptic), Planescape (the Planes of Existence), and Urban Arcana (modern-day Earth).

Of GURPS, I like Infinite Worlds (multiversal cops) and Bunnies and Burrows (rabbits with martial arts and psychic powers).

I also like Call of Cthulhu’s Delta Green, which features an ex-government organisation combating the Mythos.

I’m not very fond of the World of Darkness’s setting. It’s just much too bleak for me.

(Of course, I also love the setting of the Sentinel Comics RPG, but I specifically excluded it from the question because I figure that all of us would choose it.)

I guess we can take that little incident as further proof that my tenure as Questioner isn’t being resumed. Too difficult for me to remember something that doesn’t come with continual prompting. As for the incomplete answer, it was meant to be Nobilis. I have huge issues with the rules and worldbuilding, but in pure creative terms, it actually outstrips the WOD’s Changeling subsets in terms of beauty, tragedy poetic symbolism, and just all around coolness. There are probably settings I would like more, but few of them I’ve actually looked at.

If the WOD is too depressing, you should look at Mummy the Resurrection, which was intentionally designed as a ray of hope in the setting’s typical gloom. Naturally it didn’t sell that well, but my copy is still prominently displayed on a shelf, waiting to see actual play someday. There are a couple others that can be spun much more positively, but Mummy is probably the only one where it’s true as the default.

The_Justifier:

I guess we can take that little incident as further proof that my tenure as Questioner isn’t being resumed.

With great power, there must also come — great responsibility! Worry not, for few can carry the burden of the Questioneer.

I looked a bit into Nobilis and Mummy: The Resurrection. The latter does indeed seem more hopeful than the WoD’s other gamelines (judging by my very limited exposure to them). Plus, I do like Egyptian mythology (as evidenced by my like of Sentinels’ Ra).

And I must admit, Nobilis does seem quite intriguing. Playing as the anthropomorphic personification of some concept, any concept is certainly a unique premise. (Incidentally, it does remind me of Sentinels’ Singular Entities.) I doubt, though, that my gaming group would be as enthusiastic about it as I.

Yeah, I wasn’t recommending Nobilis overall, it’s extremely weird and disturbing (the Nobles are kind of inevitably evil/monstrous by their nature, I forget the exact details), it’s just the best fit for the very specific question you asked. My top 10 RPG settings are pretty much all either D&D campaign worlds or WOD sublines, so having to treat those as a single answer ruled out most of the alternatives I know personally.

The_Justifier:

Yeah, I wasn’t recommending Nobilis overall, it’s extremely weird and disturbing (the Nobles are kind of inevitably evil/monstrous by their nature, I forget the exact details)

I’ll take your word for it.

The_Justifier:

it’s just the best fit for the very specific question you asked. My top 10 RPG settings are pretty much all either D&D campaign worlds or WOD sublines, so having to treat those as a single answer ruled out most of the alternatives I know personally.

No, you don’t have to treat those as single answers. My answer, for example, listed three individual D&D settings. As I said above, “Game does not equal setting. A single RPG can offer multiple settings.”

Okay well in that case, Ravenloft, Planescape, Eberron, Council of Wyrms, Changeling the Lost, Kindred of the East (most especially the Ten Thousand Hells), Mummy the Resurrection, Mummy the Curse, Werewolf the Apocalypse, and the Dark Kingdom of Jade from Wraith.

Oh and I probably should have listed Exalted rather than Nobilis, because I have similar familiarity levels and Exalted is made of pure awesome, instead of the kinda subtle and kinda horrible thing Nobilis does.

Question: when was the last time you actually had an interesting game against Wager Master?

Answer: Three times today!

Screenshot_20220930-094034720×1600 111 KB

Starts with Who Are You Fighting, The New Deal, An Unwise Wager, and Playing Dice with the Cosmos, along with a Wageling or two. Unable to win by beating him up, the heroes beat themselves up instead to try and make Losing to the Odds an instant win when it appears. But then What Do You Really Know shows up, and across several turns the heroes get thrashed, until finally Idealist drops to 4 HP. Now Losing to the Odds shows up and kills her, and I don’t even bother trying to work around the impending Playing Dice trigger; I just fast forward so I can get my picture and try again.

Screenshot_20220930-140936720×1600 112 KB

This game started with similar cards on Wags’s side, but no Playing Dice this time. We did much better, and seemed poised to beat him this time…up until Harpy took the Unwise Wager (and unlike in past instances, this wasn’t due to the Ancient Tome issue, she actually did draw her entire deck because I didn’t notice what was happening in time to stop it). I’m sure there’s a story here…

Screenshot_20220930-170057720×1600 104 KB

Despite getting a reroll every time, Wags still had Who Are You Fighting, The New Deal, and An Unwise Wager at start of game! The heroes really struggled this time, with Wraith running multiple IREPs and Guise borrowing them to repeatedly hit Wags’s deck, all to ensure Playing Dice and What Do You Know didn’t see play. Wags was thrashed down to single digits while flipped, but got Who Are You Fighting back just in time to survive; the heroes then flailed helplessly, getting the snot kicked out of them by the New Deal while trying to come up with a plan. Iddy lost to the odds again due to her low HP, and the surviving heroes frantically scrambled to reshuffle their decks before an Unwise Wager could flip back up. But finally we managed to juggle Applied Numerology just right, reducing the New Deal damage for the two male heroes but not for the two women, so that we could finally make Wags be the one who Lost to the Odds.

Whew! That’s what you call earning a victory!

The_Justifier:

Question: when was the last time you actually had an interesting game against Wager Master?

Honestly, my table plays ol’ Wagey so few times that I can hardly remember any games against him.
I used to think he sucked, but the app has really helped me to understand how he’s actually meant to function, and I’ve had a lot more good experiences with him since.

I may, from time to time, post a question in this thread if I have one

You get one magic spell, which you can cast once per day. What would you want it to do?

Alternatively, what spell effect would most match your personality, general identity, and/or characteristics, but might not necessarily be the spell that you’d most like?

And please try to avoid overpowered effects. Nothing godlike or on a world scale. (I’m looking at you, world peace spell.) And no infinities or absolutes.

Teleport. Even if it’s just line of sight, the ability to get from the base of a cliff to the top of it, without having to walk all the way around the hill to where it slopes and then slowly climb up it…there are perhaps better effects to have, but this is the one I’ve regularly wished for in my real life for years.

As to reflecting me personally, well you said I wasn’t allowed to godmod… but seriously, the power to conjure small objects out of nothing and then have them dissipate would solve so much of my clutter issue. “Where the heck is my can opener”, etc.

Manifest ten U.S. $100 bills. Enough to live on comfortably and give me the freedom not to need to commute and work many hours of the day.

I don’t know how involved the spell is, though. Is it a ritual that takes some time and sacrifice? If we’re just saying no strings I stick with my answer. Not trying to get too greedy, but it’s true when it’s said time is money.

Thunderbird:

it’s true when it’s said time is money.

So why not just wish for the power to create more time?

That sounds like god mode. Things start getting real weird when you mess with time. And odds are I’d screw it up somehow and have too much time with nothing to occupy it, or somehow short myself and just constantly be run ragged.

Thunderbird:

That sounds like god mode.

Valid; I don’t think a few extra hours in the day are unreasonable, but if you can do a five second ritual to step into Hammerspace for an hour, and there’s no restriction against doing it again when the hour is up, then that’s obviously an issue. There’d have to be some cost or limit to it.

Things start getting real weird when you mess with time.

Only really true if you can travel backwards in time (which would probably be impossible even with superpowers, just as making 2 plus 2 equal 5 is probably impossible even if you’re literally omnipotent). Time extension shouldn’t cause major problems as long as you set your various timepieces to account for it. Nothing about our lives would break if we all lived on Bajor and had a 26-hour day; at worst, one person having extremely high tier time extension would be able to break the economy, but only if that was what he actively tried to do.

And odds are I’d screw it up somehow and have too much time with nothing to occupy it

Not a problem I’ll ever have…at least as long as I have enough phone battery power to play Sentinels of the Multiverse: The Video Game! (I didn’t start this post intending it to be hamfisted product placement, but here we are.)

Teleportation and money-conjuring both sound pretty useful to me, although the latter seems fairly boring. I think I’d rather have a spell that would let me hire myself out.

The_Justifier:

you said I wasn’t allowed to godmod… but seriously, the power to conjure small objects out of nothing and then have them dissipate would solve so much of my clutter issue.

I think that that would be allowable.

Not really, as far as I imagined it. I’m thinking that all the spell requires is an arcane word or phrase, a snap of the fingers or a series of gestures, or perhaps just a thought.

Yeah, I am of the opinion that messing with time is likely to be non-permissible. Although something small and simple like “Everything except for me pauses for an hour” might work, but not anything beyond that.

The_Justifier:

if you can do a five second ritual to step into Hammerspace for an hour, and there’s no restriction against doing it again when the hour is up, then that’s obviously an issue. There’d have to be some cost or limit to it.

QotD: Soothsayer Carmichael knows everything he would need to know in order to perform magic, yet he can’t perform magic. Whatever the thing you use to perform magic is, let’s say for the sake of argument that it’s a specific portion of your soul…he just plain doesn’t have that portion. Would you be okay with saying that this qualifies him as a disabled person, and writing several stories in which he’s used as an analogy for being blind or deaf or mute, in the same way that X-Men stories are often analogies for racist or LGBT issues?

Hmm, interesting query, that. I’m inclined to say no, as I personally define a disability as something that prevents one from doing something that the average person frequently does; not something that prevents one from doing something exceptional and extraordinary.

Like, for example, I wouldn’t say that someone who can’t curl their tongue has a disability, or someone who for whatever reason can’t give blood transfusions, as those aren’t really typical activities. It’s kind of like not having photographic (or eidetic) memory; all it does is prevent you from doing the extraordinary, not the ordinary.

I suppose, however, that this does depend on the rarity in the population of the Sentinels Universe of that portion of the soul, that potential to do magic. (Which, for brevity’s sake, I’m just gonna call Magery, as that’s what a similar concept is called in the GURPS RPG.) If most folks do possess Magery, but just have never learned how to harness it (for obvious reasons), then I suppose Carmichael’s situation could be likened to being, say, someone who’s tone-deaf and yet wants to be a singer—he can’t learn to do this one thing that most people could, but it’s still not a super common or necessary life skill.

But, if Magery is actually very rare in the populace, then it’s more like the analogy I used before: photographic memory, a rare trait that the lack of having only really affects you if you want to go into a profession that requires it. (I don’t actually know if any professions require photographic memory, but whatevs.)

So, which one is it? How common is Magery in Sentinels? Well, let’s look at the evidence: Soothsayer C. is literally the only character we know of who has this condition; every other character who’s tried to learn magic in SC has been able to do so. There could be some sampling bias in this, of course, as we only really see the stories of exceptional people.

Of course, this is all going about things from the Watsonian perspective. The Doylist answer would probably just be “Write whatever story you want, as long as it makes some amount of sense.” (And that last bit ain’t even necessary.)

Another thing is that the “mutants as minorities” thing isn’t 100% logical either. E.g., Gay people can’t mind control the President or blow up a whole city.

posts.name: Trajector
posts.cooked:
Robert Hooke! Read a fascinating dual biography of him and Edmund Halley called “Out of the Shadow of a Giant.” Hooke is known today almost solely for Hooke’s Law, which governs the relationship between force and displacement in springs. But he was the Royal Society’s experimentalist in residence and came up with all kinds of physics demonstrations and observations, including a good fraction of the stuff credited to Sir Isaac Newton! Hooke even realized the inverse square law of gravity and the idea that gravity is a property of mass before Newton did. In fact, Newton probably came up with his story about the apple as an obfuscation to claim credit for the idea first, and had such a fued with Hooke that, after Hooke’s death, Newton ordered the only portrait of him destroyed. Newton’s famous quote, “if I have seen further, it is because I have stood on the shoulders of giants” was actually a dig at Hooke, who was very short.

In summary, Isaac Newton was a jerk and Robert Hooke laid the real foundations of experimental physics, thank you for coming to my TED Talk.

(Halley was also fascinating…as a wealthy patron of science he bought a ship and crew, made himself captain, and sailed around doing scientific expeditions.)

QotD: Who is a historical figure who you think is obscure and underappreciated?

My answer is undoubtedly Dr. William Thornton. He was an American physician and polymath from the late 1700s and the early 1800s, and an all-around radical guy; here’s a brief overview:

  • He was a steampunk inventor, having designed a steamboat boiler, a steam-powered gun, and a steam-powered organ that would be heard throughout a whole city.
  • He grew up on a slave-worked plantation, yet he was staunchly abolitionist; he proposed a colony in Africa where freed slaves could go to escape persecution; his ideas eventually influenced the founding of the country of Liberia.
  • He won the contest to design the U.S. Capitol Building and the White House, despite having zero formal training in architecture; his designs were just that much more majestic than those of the other contestants, even those who were actual architects.
  • He was good friends with George Washington. When Washington died, Thornton wanted to attempt to bring him back from the dead using science! But for some reason no one let him try.
Quote from Thornton about Washington's death, 1819

“My feelings at that moment I cannot express! I was overwhelmed with the loss of the best friend I had on Earth . . . The weather was very cold, & [George Washington] remained in a frozen state, for several Days. I proposed to attempt his restoration, in the following manner. First to thaw him in cold water, then to lay him in blankets, & by degrees & by friction to give him warmth, and to put into activity the minute blood vessels, at the same time to open a passage to the Lungs by the Trachaea, and to inflate them with air, to produce an artificial respiration, and to transfuse blood into him from a lamb. If these means had been resorted to, & had failed all that could be done would have been done, but I was not seconded in this proposal; for it was deemed unavailing. I reasoned thus. He died by the loss of blood & the want of air. Restore these with the heat that had subsequently been deducted, and as the organization was in every respect perfect, there was no doubt in my mind that his restoration was possible.”

  • He was the first Superintendent of the U.S. Patent Office, and during the War of 1812’s Burning of Washington D.C., pretty much every building in the capitol was destroyed…except the Patent Office, because Thornton convinced the attacking soldiers not to.
Quote from R. Beresford, 1886, about Thornton's saving of the Patent Office

“A story is told of [William Thornton] that, during the war of 1812, when the British captured the city of Washington and destroyed the Capitol building, a loaded cannon was trained upon the Patent Office for the purpose of destroying it, and he is said to have put himself before the gun, and in a frenzy of excitement exclaimed: ‘Are you Englishmen or only Goths and Vandals? This is the Patent Office, a depository of the ingenuity of the American nation, in which the whole civilized world is interested. Would you destroy it? If so, fire away, and let the charge pass through my body.’ The effect is said to have been magical upon the soldiers, and to have saved the Patent Office from destruction.”

So, yeah. William Thornton was rad, and way cooler than Alexander Hamilton.

My normal answer would be a nice strawberry jam without too much added sugar so that I can still taste the strawberries.

That said, a (very nice) jam place near my work makes an orange marmelade that is so fantastically good that my taste buds seem to have forgotten that I don’t normally like marmelade!

On the jelly front, a nice red pepper jelly with some spiciness coming through is The Best Thing to have with some crackers and cheese.
A nice peach jelly or orange marmalade is nice.

posts.name: Chief Lackey Rich
posts.cooked: Marmalade on a buttered English muffin or nothing. Spent my entire elementary school being fed peanut better and grape jelly sandwiches every single day by my incompetent caregivers and it’s pretty well put me off on both jams and jellies for life, but I associate orange marmalade with Christmas mornings (the only time we ever saw the stuff) and it’s escaped my distaste because of it.

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked: I’ll almost always prefer Jam. I like the sensation that there might actually be fruit in it.
Marionberry.

So I dunno if this is fate or just a digital hiccup, but this topic just registered as unread for me, even though I was active on the forum for like six months after the last post here. Maybe, with >G basically shutting down, we shouldn’t try to use this board, but alternatively, with C&A scrambling to try and re-house the IP, this is the right time for the community to show potential investors that we’re still here and still passionate.

Oh, and on the topic of Fjur’s last question, I wouldn’t call it my favorite, but the unquestionable most interesting fruit preserves I have at the moment is a Chocolate Cherry jam from a farmer’s market here in the Midwest. I also have gooseberry, but haven’t tried that one yet; the black forest flavor is quite remarkable, although a little dark and bitter for my preference.

(If you insist that I have to ask a new question, then it shall be “Should we continue?”)
